summary.title: Task Manager API
summary.description:
STRIDE threat model for github.com/ghiwet/Task-Manager-API: Spring Boot 4 API with Keycloak OIDC/JWT, PostgreSQL RLS multi-tenancy, Kafka transactional outbox, Redis cache + rate limiting, Elasticsearch search, pgvector RAG assistant (OpenAI), OTel/Grafana observability, delivered via GitHub Actions, GHCR, Terraform, Argo CD and Sealed Secrets.

Scope: runtime request/data flows and the delivery pipeline. Built from the README; Open threats need verification against code and config.

diagrams.title: 1. Runtime: request and event flows
diagrams.description: API, identity, data stores, event pipeline, AI assistant, observability.

threats.title: Credential stuffing / brute force on login
threats.description: Attackers replay leaked passwords against the Keycloak login and the local /api/v1/users/register user store.
threats.mitigation: Enable Keycloak brute-force detection and offer MFA (OTP/WebAuthn). Apply the same lockout/throttling to any local-password login path.

threats.title: Admin destructive actions not auditable
threats.description: Admins can delete any task or user in the tenant and reset any user's password. Without an audit trail an admin can deny doing so, and incidents can't be reconstructed.
threats.mitigation: Fixed: new audit_log table (V8 migration) records actor/tenant/action/target/traceId for admin cross-user task deletes, user deletes, and password resets, written inside the same transaction as the change. app_rls has only INSERT+SELECT on the table (explicit REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE, overriding V5's blanket default-privilege grant), so a compromised app session can't rewrite history. New GET /api/v1/audit (admin-only, tenant-scoped via RLS) to read it. Verified: integration tests prove both that cross-user admin actions create the expected row and that app_rls genuinely cannot UPDATE/DELETE an existing row (direct JDBC assertion, not just that the app never tries).

data.name:
React SPA
(browser)
data.description: Vite + TS SPA, Keycloak OIDC Auth Code + PKCE (public client taskmanager-spa), TanStack Query.

threats.title: Stored XSS via search highlight fragments
threats.description: Elasticsearch highlight fragments are wrapped in <em> tags around user-controlled task text; TaskSearchService.java already sets HighlightParameters encoder=html (verified in code), so a matched fragment is safe to render via dangerouslySetInnerHTML. The remaining gap: TasksView.tsx renders r.highlights[0] ?? r.title through the same dangerouslySetInnerHTML call, and when a hit has no highlight fragment for either field it falls back to the raw, unescaped task title -- that fallback path is not covered by the encoder fix and remains exploitable.
threats.mitigation: Primary vector is mitigated (HighlightParameters.withEncoder('html') in TaskSearchService.java). Close the remaining gap by escaping or textContent-rendering the r.title fallback in TasksView.tsx instead of passing it to dangerouslySetInnerHTML, and add a strict CSP on the SPA host (script-src 'self', no unsafe-inline) as defense in depth.

threats.title: Tokens readable by injected script
threats.description: OIDC tokens kept in localStorage/sessionStorage by the OIDC client library are readable by any XSS on the SPA origin.
threats.mitigation: Keep tokens in memory, use short access-token lifetimes and refresh-token rotation in Keycloak, or move to a BFF with HttpOnly session cookies.

threats.title: Unsafe rendering of AI assistant answers
threats.description: The assistant answer is model output that can echo attacker-influenced task text. Rendering it as Markdown/HTML without sanitization is an XSS sink.
threats.mitigation: Treat LLM output as untrusted: render as text or sanitize Markdown output (e.g. DOMPurify).

data.name: Keycloak
data.description: Issues JWTs with custom tenant_id claim (user attribute + protocol mapper). Brokers Google/GitHub.

threats.title: User-editable tenant_id attribute enables tenant hopping
threats.description: tenant_id is a Keycloak user attribute mapped into the JWT, and RLS trusts it completely. If the realm's User Profile allows users to edit attributes (account console / unmanaged attributes policy), a user can set their own tenant_id to another tenant and get full access to that tenant's data.
threats.mitigation: Fixed: realm-export.json now declares an explicit User Profile config (components.org.keycloak.userprofile.UserProfileProvider) with tenant_id permissions view/edit restricted to admin only, and unmanagedAttributePolicy set to ADMIN_EDIT. The existing username/email/firstName/lastName attributes keep their original validations (length, email format, prohibited-characters, homograph) so declaring the profile explicitly doesn't silently drop Keycloak's own defaults. Verified: re-imported into a fresh Keycloak and confirmed via the Admin API (GET /admin/realms/myrealm/users/profile) that tenant_id resolves to admin-only view/edit, and that a normal login still succeeds with the tenant_id claim intact.

threats.title: Loose redirect URIs / web origins on public client
threats.description: Wildcard redirect URIs or web origins '*' on the public SPA client allow authorization codes or tokens to be delivered to an attacker-controlled page.
threats.mitigation: Use exact redirect URIs per environment, explicit web origins, enforce PKCE S256 on the client, and disable implicit flow and direct access grants for taskmanager-spa.

threats.title: Keycloak admin console exposed
threats.description: If the master realm admin console is reachable through the same ingress as the login endpoints, it becomes an internet-facing high-value target (default admin credentials in dev compose).
threats.mitigation: Expose only /realms/* publicly; restrict /admin to an internal network; rotate bootstrap admin credentials and require MFA for admins.

data.name:
Task Manager API
(Spring Boot)
data.description: /api/v1 REST, JWT resource server, TenantFilter -> set_config(app.current_tenant), Bucket4j, cache-aside, RAG assistant (Spring AI), OutboxRelay.

threats.title: JWT audience not validated
threats.description: Spring's resource server validates signature, exp and issuer, but not 'aud' unless configured. Any token issued by the realm to another client (e.g. a different app) is accepted by the API.
threats.mitigation: Configure spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences (or a custom OAuth2TokenValidator) to require the API's audience; add an audience mapper in Keycloak.

threats.title: Intra-tenant BOLA/IDOR on task and user endpoints
threats.description: RLS blocks cross-tenant access, but ownership within a tenant (GET/PUT/DELETE /tasks/{id}, PUT /users/{username}) relies on application checks. A missed check lets a user read or modify a colleague's tasks.
threats.mitigation: Enforce ownership in the service/repository layer (not only controllers), and add parameterized authorization tests per endpoint x role (owner, other user same tenant, admin).

threats.title: Self-registration tenant assignment
threats.description: POST /api/v1/users/register is public. If the request or a default decides the new user's tenant, an attacker can register into an existing customer's tenant.
threats.mitigation: Never accept tenant from the registration body; assign tenants only via invitation/admin provisioning in Keycloak, or create a fresh tenant per self-signup.

threats.title: Password change without re-authentication
threats.description: PUT /api/v1/users/{username} updates a password; if it doesn't require the current password, a stolen access token becomes a permanent account takeover.
threats.mitigation: Require the current password (or Keycloak re-auth / step-up) for self-service changes; route password management to Keycloak where possible.

threats.title: Username enumeration on registration (incl. cross-tenant)
threats.description: Registration returns 409 Conflict for existing usernames, letting an attacker enumerate accounts. Cross-tenant variant: AppUserService.registerNewUser checks findByUsername under RLS, so it only sees the caller's tenant, while users.username is globally UNIQUE. Registering a name that exists in another tenant passes the check, then fails on the UNIQUE constraint with a DataIntegrityViolationException that GlobalExceptionHandler does not map, so it surfaces as a 500. The 201 / 409 / 500 split tells a caller whether a username exists in their own tenant, in another tenant, or nowhere.
threats.mitigation: Accept the risk with the strict register rate limit, or return a generic response and notify out of band. For the cross-tenant variant: decide whether usernames are global or per-tenant. If global, do the existence check with a tenant-agnostic query (SECURITY DEFINER function returning a boolean) and map DataIntegrityViolationException to the same generic response; if per-tenant, change the constraint to UNIQUE (tenant_id, username). Either way the response must not differ between the in-tenant and cross-tenant cases.

threats.title: Mass assignment of id/version/roles
threats.description: Binding the request body to the entity would let callers set roles or ids.
threats.mitigation: Registration binds a dedicated UserRegistrationDto with Bean Validation (documented in README).

threats.title: Rate limiter fails open when Redis is down
threats.description: The Bucket4j filter allows all requests if Redis is unavailable. An attacker who can degrade Redis (or during an outage) gets unlimited registration attempts and unlimited assistant calls (OpenAI cost).
threats.mitigation: Keep fail-open for normal reads but fail closed (or fall back to a small local in-memory bucket) for /users/register and /assistant/query; alert on the fallback.

threats.title: X-Forwarded-For spoofing bypasses anonymous rate limit
threats.description: Anonymous requests are keyed by client IP and the filter is X-Forwarded-For aware. If XFF is trusted from any source, an attacker rotates the header to get a fresh bucket per request on /users/register.
threats.mitigation: Only honour XFF from the ingress (server.forward-headers-strategy=native with internal-proxies set, or take the right-most untrusted hop) and strip client-supplied XFF at the ingress.

threats.title: Actuator endpoints exposed
threats.description: Actuator (health details, prometheus, possibly env/heapdump/loggers) on the main port is reachable through the ingress. Heap dumps contain tokens and secrets.
threats.mitigation: Move actuator to a separate management port not exposed by the ingress, expose only health/info/prometheus, hide health details from anonymous users.

threats.title: RLS-bypassing migration credentials in the app pod
threats.description: The app connects as app_rls, but Flyway runs at startup as the owner role (spring.flyway.user), so the owner/superuser credentials sit in the same pod's environment. Any RCE, SSRF-to-env, or heap dump yields credentials that bypass RLS for all tenants.
threats.mitigation: Partially addressed: Flyway now runs in a dedicated Helm migration Job (new spring.profiles.active=migrate, excludes OAuth2/Spring AI autoconfig, MigrationExitRunner calls SpringApplication.exit) with its own migration-secret/SealedSecret holding SPRING_FLYWAY_PASSWORD; the app Secret/ConfigMap no longer carry SPRING_FLYWAY_* at all, and the Deployment explicitly sets SPRING_FLYWAY_ENABLED=false. Argo CD sync-waves order the Job (wave 0) before the Deployment (wave 1). Verified: helm lint/template render correctly in both plaintext and GitOps (secrets.create=false) modes, and a local run with -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=migrate against the real Postgres migrated cleanly and exited 0. Still open (reopened after AppSec review): src/main/resources/application.properties still ships spring.flyway.user=taskuser / spring.flyway.password=taskpass inside the app jar, and taskpass is also the deployed owner password (terraform backing-services variables.tf default, helm values.yaml flywayPassword). Anyone who can read the app pod's classpath or a config/env dump (RCE, /actuator if env is exposed, heap dump) still gets RLS-bypassing credentials. Remaining fix: remove the Flyway credentials from application.properties (supply them only via the migration Job's env, or a dev-only profile/compose env), and rotate the owner password away from the dev default in Terraform/the migration SealedSecret.

threats.title: Denial of wallet on AI assistant
threats.description: Repeated /assistant/query calls drive OpenAI token spend.
threats.mitigation: Separate stricter assistant rate-limit bucket, Resilience4j timeout/circuit breaker, token-usage metrics (README). Residual risk: see fail-open threat; add an OpenAI spend limit and an alert on gen_ai_client_token_usage_total.

threats.title: Indirect prompt injection via task content
threats.description: Task text retrieved into the prompt can contain instructions. Retrieval is limited to the caller's own tasks, so impact is mostly self-inflicted today, but it grows if tools/actions or shared tasks are added.
threats.mitigation: Keep the assistant read-only (no tool calling), delimit retrieved context clearly in the system prompt, and validate retrievedTaskIds server-side against the caller.

threats.title: Callers without a tenant_id share the '__unresolved__' fallback tenant
threats.description: TenantContext.getTenantId() returns the sentinel '__unresolved__' when no tenant is bound. TenantFilter only reads the tenant_id claim from a JwtAuthenticationToken, so every JWT missing the claim (a Keycloak user without the attribute, service-account or Swagger tokens) and every oauth2Login browser session runs as '__unresolved__'. RLS default-denies reads of real tenants, but the sentinel is itself writable: services stamp tenant_id='__unresolved__' on insert and the WITH CHECK policy accepts it. All such unrelated callers therefore share one tenant, and an admin among them can list (/tasks/all, /users) and delete the others' data.
threats.mitigation: Fixed: TenantFilter now fails closed -- an authenticated /api/** request with no resolvable tenant (JWT missing tenant_id, a tenant_id claim equal to the sentinel, or an oauth2Login session, which carries no JWT) is rejected with 403 problem+json instead of running under '__unresolved__'; unauthenticated requests still get 401 from Spring Security. Database backstop: Flyway V10 adds CHECK (tenant_id <> '__unresolved__') NOT VALID to tasks, users, audit_log and vector_store, so no code path (background job, startup runner, future endpoint) can write into the sentinel; NOT VALID keeps the migration safe on dev DBs that already hold sentinel rows, which stay unreachable. The startup CommandLineRunner that seeded local 'user'/'admin' (ROLE_ADMIN) rows -- which always landed in '__unresolved__' -- was removed. Verified: TenantIsolationTest (app connected as app_rls) asserts 403 for a tenant-less JWT and for a sentinel-valued claim, 401 for no token, and a DataIntegrityViolationException when inserting a sentinel row with the sentinel GUC bound; full suite green (77 tests); live run against a fresh DB migrated to v10, a real Keycloak user1 token created a task stamped tenant-a (201), and no seeded users were created.

threats.title: Unbounded metric cardinality from raw request URI tag
threats.description: RateLimitFilter tags the rate.limit.exceeded.total counter with request.getRequestURI(), which the client controls. Once throttled, an anonymous client can request /x/<random> repeatedly; each distinct path registers a new Micrometer meter, growing heap use and the /actuator/prometheus payload (and Prometheus TSDB series) without bound.
threats.mitigation: Tag with a bounded value: the matched route template (BEST_MATCHING_PATTERN_ATTRIBUTE) or the bucket/key type only, never the raw URI. Optionally add a MeterFilter.maximumAllowableTags guard on rate.limit.exceeded.total.

threats.title: Unbounded task description size
threats.description: TaskCreateDto.description has no @Size limit (title is capped at 255). An authenticated user within the 60 req/min limit can store multi-MB descriptions, which then inflate the outbox row, the Kafka message, ONNX embedding work, the Elasticsearch document, consumer logs and the OpenAI prompt (token cost), slowing consumers or pushing messages to the DLT.
threats.mitigation: Add @Size(max = ...) on description (and a matching column/DB CHECK limit), cap spring.servlet multipart/request body size at the ingress and in Tomcat, and truncate retrieved context before building the LLM prompt.

threats.title: Background job runs outside tenant context
threats.description: The relay reads outbox rows of all tenants. If it connects with the owner role to bypass RLS, that role is also available to the rest of the code path; if it uses app_rls with no tenant set, RLS returns nothing (default deny).
threats.mitigation: Give the relay (and consumers) a dedicated DB role whose BYPASSRLS / policy grant covers only the outbox table, or iterate per tenant with SET LOCAL app.current_tenant.

threats.title: Poison messages block processing
threats.description: A malformed event could make consumers retry forever.
threats.mitigation: Dead-letter topic and idempotent upserts by deterministic id (README).

threats.title: Consumers trust event payload for tenant and content
threats.description: Consumers write embeddings and search documents based on event fields. A forged event (see Kafka) can plant content or task ids into another tenant's vector store / index, which then shows up in that tenant's search and RAG answers.
threats.mitigation: Fixed: TaskEmbeddingService.upsert now reloads title/description/owner from Postgres on the same tenant-bound JDBC connection (RLS-scoped) instead of trusting the event, skipping if no row is found. TaskSearchIndexService.upsert reloads the Task via TaskRepository under the event's claimed tenant (TenantContext) and indexes the DB row, not the payload; delete checks the existing TaskDocument's own tenantId against the event's before deleting (ES has no RLS to lean on for that case). Verified: full Maven suite green (63/63), including a new TaskSearchIndexTest case asserting a forged event with no backing row indexes nothing, and AssistantRetrievalIsolationTest updated to persist real rows before upserting.

threats.title: Cross-tenant read via missing WHERE clause
threats.description: A query that forgets the tenant filter could return other tenants' rows.
threats.mitigation: Row-level security with USING/WITH CHECK on tenant_id, app connects as non-owner app_rls, missing tenant = default deny, TenantIsolationTest (README).

threats.title: Tenant context leaks across pooled connections
threats.description: set_config on a pooled connection that isn't reset (exception path, async/virtual threads, @Async, connection reused outside Hibernate) serves the next request with the previous tenant.
threats.mitigation: Prefer transaction-scoped SET LOCAL everywhere (as the RAG path does), add a test that fails a request mid-transaction and checks the next borrow, and assert tenant on connection borrow.

threats.title: Unencrypted JDBC and data at rest
threats.description: JDBC without TLS inside the cluster and unencrypted volumes/backups expose all tenants' data to anyone with network or storage access.
threats.mitigation: sslmode=verify-full, encrypted storage class and backups, NetworkPolicy allowing only the API/migration pods to reach 5432.

threats.title: Cached reads bypass RLS; cache key lacks tenant; admin delete leaves stale entry
threats.description: findTask is cached under owner:id and served from Redis without touching Postgres, so RLS does not protect cached reads. The README notes the same owner can exist in two tenants; isolation then depends on ids never colliding. A tenant change in Keycloak also keeps serving old-tenant tasks until TTL. Stale-entry variant: TaskService.deleteTask evicts key '#owner:#id' where #owner is the caller, so when an admin deletes another user's task (findById path) the admin's key is evicted, not the owner's. The owner's cached copy survives and GET /api/v1/tasks/{id} keeps returning the deleted task for up to the cache TTL (cache.tasks.ttl-minutes, 10 min).
threats.mitigation: Fixed: the task cache key is now tenant:owner:id, built in one place (TaskService.cacheKey, tenant from TenantContext) and shared by @Cacheable(findTask) and @CacheEvict(updateTask) via SpEL, so the same owner name in two tenants, or a user whose tenant changed, can no longer be served another tenant's cached task. deleteTask no longer uses @CacheEvict keyed on the caller: it evicts programmatically after the lookup, under the task's actual owner, so an admin deleting another user's task clears the owner's entry. The programmatic eviction fails open (logged, delete still succeeds) like the annotated operations under LoggingCacheErrorHandler. Old owner:id entries are never read again and expire with the TTL. Verified: CacheIntegrationTest asserts the tenant-scoped key, that an admin delete evicts the owner's entry and the owner then gets TaskNotFound, and that another tenant's key for the same owner/id is a miss; full suite green (79 tests); live run with real Keycloak tokens: user2 read cached under tenant-b:user2:<id>, admin1 (same tenant) DELETE 204 removed the key, and user2's next GET returned 404.

threats.title: Unauthenticated Redis: cache poisoning and limit reset
threats.description: Without AUTH/ACLs any pod in the cluster can overwrite cached task objects (served to users as truth) or delete rate-limit buckets. If JDK serialization is used for values, writing a gadget payload can become RCE in the API.
threats.mitigation: Enable Redis ACL user + TLS, NetworkPolicy to API pods only, and use a JSON serializer (GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer with a restricted type validator) instead of JDK serialization.

threats.title: Tenant isolation enforced only in query code
threats.description: Elasticsearch has no RLS, so tenant isolation depends entirely on every query adding a tenant filter. Verified in code: both /search and /search/all (TaskSearchController -> TaskSearchService) always apply TenantContext.getTenantId() as a filter -- only the owner filter is dropped for admin -- so there is no live cross-tenant leak today. The risk is structural: a future search endpoint that forgets the tenant filter has no RLS-equivalent backstop to catch it.
threats.mitigation: Centralize query building so the tenant filter cannot be omitted (a single search entrypoint that always injects it), or use per-tenant filtered aliases/indices; add an ES tenant-isolation integration test (Testcontainers) that fails if a new endpoint omits the filter.

threats.title: Elasticsearch security disabled
threats.description: With xpack security off, any pod can read or rewrite the whole index.
threats.mitigation: Enable security, a least-privilege API key for the app (read/write on the task index only), TLS, and NetworkPolicy.

threats.title: Expensive query syntax from user input
threats.description: If q is passed into query_string, users can submit leading wildcards/regex that are costly.
threats.mitigation: Use match/multi_match or simple_query_string, cap q length, set request timeouts.

threats.title: Forged events from any pod (PLAINTEXT, no ACLs)
threats.description: If brokers accept PLAINTEXT connections without authentication or ACLs, anything in the cluster (or kafka-ui) can produce task-events for any tenant.
threats.mitigation: Fixed: broker now requires SASL_PLAINTEXT/SCRAM-SHA-512 in both docker-compose and the Terraform backing-services module. A one-shot kafka-init step (docker-compose service / k8s initContainer) seeds SCRAM credentials for the inter-broker, taskmanager-app and kafka-ui principals directly at kafka-storage.sh format time (--add-scram, KIP-900), avoiding any temporary unauthenticated listener. StandardAuthorizer is enabled with those principals (plus ANONYMOUS, needed only for the never-externally-exposed intra-cluster CONTROLLER listener) as super users -- default-deny for everyone else. Spring Kafka client config and kafka-ui both carry matching SASL credentials. Verified live: kafka-init seeded all three credentials, an unauthenticated kafka-topics.sh client hung/timed out, an authenticated one succeeded, kafka-ui and the app's own producer/consumer-group connections logged in successfully.

threats.title: Task data retained in DLT and visible in kafka-ui
threats.description: Dead-lettered events keep full task content indefinitely, and kafka-ui (no auth in compose) shows all tenants' messages and can publish new ones.
threats.mitigation: Set retention on the DLT, carry ids instead of task text in events, and keep kafka-ui out of shared environments or put it behind SSO.

threats.title: Lost or duplicated events
threats.description: Dual writes could lose events or desync derived stores.
threats.mitigation: Transactional outbox, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED relay, idempotent consumers (README).

threats.title: Sensitive data in traces and logs
threats.description: With sampling 1.0, JDBC spans, Kafka spans and Spring AI observations can carry SQL parameters, task text, prompts/completions or headers into Tempo and logs, outside RLS.
threats.mitigation: Keep Spring AI prompt/completion logging off, disable JDBC parameter capture, never log Authorization headers, and lower sampling in production.

threats.title: Default/absent auth on observability UIs
threats.description: Grafana admin/admin and unauthenticated Prometheus/Tempo/Alertmanager let anyone with network access read operational data or silence alerts.
threats.mitigation: Change Grafana admin password via Secret, SSO for Grafana, keep Prometheus/Tempo/Alertmanager internal-only.

threats.title: Account takeover via automatic account linking
threats.description: If Keycloak's first-broker-login flow auto-links a federated identity to an existing user by email, an attacker with a GitHub account using the victim's (unverified) email takes over the account.
threats.mitigation: Require email verification / 'review profile + confirm link' in first-broker-login, and don't trust unverified emails from GitHub.

threats.title: OpenAI API key leakage
threats.description: Passing the key with helm --set leaves it in shell history and the Helm release secret; a leaked key enables spend abuse.
threats.mitigation: Supply it only via the SealedSecret, use a project-scoped key with a spend cap, rotate on suspicion.

threats.title: Permissive CORS
threats.description: The SPA calls the API cross-origin. A wildcard or reflected Origin with credentials lets any site use a victim's session.
threats.mitigation: Allow only the SPA origin(s) per environment, no allowCredentials with wildcard, limit methods/headers.

threats.title: Plain HTTP outside local dev
threats.description: Local setup is http://localhost; HSTS only applies over HTTPS.
threats.mitigation: Terminate TLS at the ingress for every non-local environment and redirect HTTP.

threats.title: CSRF on /api/** for session-authenticated browser requests
threats.description: WebSecurityConfig disables CSRF for /api/** on the assumption the API is Bearer-token-only, but the same SecurityFilterChain also enables oauth2Login, so a browser holding a JSESSIONID is authenticated on /api/** routes guarded only by .anyRequest().authenticated() (e.g. POST /api/v1/tasks). An attacker page can trigger state-changing requests carrying the session cookie and no CSRF token; JSON bodies currently need a CORS preflight, which limits exploitation, but any endpoint that accepts a simple (form/text) content type, or a future one, becomes exploitable.
threats.mitigation: Split into two SecurityFilterChains: an /api/** chain that is stateless and accepts only Bearer JWTs (no oauth2Login, SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS), and a browser chain for /login, /dashboard and /logout with CSRF enabled. Alternatively, keep CSRF enabled for any request authenticated by a session. Add a test that a session-cookie POST to /api/** is rejected.

threats.title: Tenant task data sent to a third-party LLM
threats.description: Task titles/descriptions are sent to OpenAI (US). For EU tenants this is a personal-data transfer requiring a DPA, transfer basis and disclosure; data may be retained by the provider.
threats.mitigation: Sign OpenAI's DPA, use zero-data-retention / EU data residency where available, document in the privacy notice, allow tenants to disable the assistant, or swap to an EU-hosted model.

diagrams.title: 2. Delivery and secrets supply chain
diagrams.description: CI/CD, image registry, GitOps, Terraform, Sealed Secrets.

threats.title: Stolen developer credentials push to main
threats.description: A compromised GitHub account can push directly; with GitOps this deploys to the cluster.
threats.mitigation: Hardware-key 2FA on GitHub, fine-grained tokens, signed commits.

threats.title: Sealed Secrets private key stored in Terraform state
threats.description: Terraform seeds the controller with a fixed keypair. The private key is gitignored, but Terraform writes it into terraform.tfstate in plaintext. Anyone with the state file (laptop backup, shared drive, CI artifact) can decrypt every SealedSecret ever committed to Git, including history.
threats.mitigation: Fixed: the sealed-secrets module no longer has a kubernetes_secret resource holding the key as a `data` attribute. Instead, a null_resource + local-exec runs `kubectl create secret tls ... | kubectl label | kubectl apply` directly against the key's file path -- the key content never becomes a Terraform attribute, only a one-way filesha256 hash (to retrigger on rotation) lands in state. Verified: `terraform validate` passes, `terraform providers` confirms the module no longer depends on the kubernetes provider at all, and the kubectl pipeline was tested end-to-end (dry-run) against a disposable test keypair. No rotation performed since this project's state was never shared externally.

Git repo (main)
Helm chart, Argo CD apps,
SealedSecrets

threats.title: Repo write access equals cluster deploy
threats.description: Argo CD auto-syncs main with prune + self-heal. Anyone who can merge to main (or a malicious PR merged without review) changes what runs in the cluster, including image tags and RBAC.
threats.mitigation: Fixed: branch protection on main already required 1 approving review + 4 status checks + no force-push; added .github/CODEOWNERS requiring the repo owner's review on /argocd/, /helm/, and .github/ itself (so the CODEOWNERS file can't be edited around), and enabled require_code_owner_reviews on the branch protection rule so it's actually enforced, not just advisory. Verified via the branch protection API that require_code_owner_reviews is true and the other settings weren't clobbered. A separate config repo remains a possible follow-up, not done here.

threats.title: Committed SealedSecrets decryptable forever
threats.description: With a fixed, never-rotated key, any leak of the key exposes all historical secrets.
threats.mitigation: Periodic key renewal and re-sealing; treat secret values as rotated if the key is suspected compromised.

threats.title: Security scans not gating merges or releases
threats.description: security.yml (CodeQL, Semgrep, Dependency-Check, TruffleHog, ZAP) runs only on manual workflow_dispatch, so vulnerable code and dependencies can be released without a scan.
threats.mitigation: Fixed: new pr-security.yml runs the fast checks (CodeQL, Semgrep, TruffleHog with --fail --only-verified) on every pull_request and push to main; branch protection on main now requires it (plus ci.yml's build-test) to pass, with 1 approving review, before merge. Dependency-Check and the ZAP baseline scan stay manual in security.yml (too slow/stateful to gate every PR). Verified: GET on the branch protection API confirms the 4 required contexts, required review count, and disabled force-push are actually live.

threats.title: Third-party actions and token permissions
threats.description: Actions referenced by mutable tags and broad GITHUB_TOKEN permissions let a compromised action push images or code.
threats.mitigation: Pin actions to commit SHAs, set permissions: read-all by default and packages: write only in release.yml, enable Dependabot for actions.

threats.title: Mutable image tags (:latest, :1.0.1)
threats.description: Argo CD pins image.tag, not a digest; anyone able to push to the package can replace the image behind an existing tag.
threats.mitigation: Partially addressed: release.yml now signs every pushed image with cosign (keyless, Fulcio/Rekor) by digest, so tampering is at least detectable. Still open: Argo CD's Application still pins image.tag, not a digest -- deferred rather than fabricated, since a real digest only exists after a real tagged release runs; the next release should switch to pinning the Application at the signed digest, and admission-time verification (Kyverno/Sigstore policy-controller) is still unimplemented.

threats.title: Argo CD admin access
threats.description: The initial admin secret stays in the cluster and the UI is reachable via port-forward; Argo CD can deploy anything cluster-wide.
threats.mitigation: Partially addressed: the argocd Terraform module now deletes argocd-initial-admin-secret right after install (a null_resource tied to the helm_release). The admin account's bcrypt hash still lives in argocd-secret (untouched), so this removes the convenient plaintext copy, not the account -- capture or rotate the password before it's deleted if you need it. Still open: no SSO/RBAC, and the AppProject still isn't restricted to the task-manager namespace/resource kinds -- Argo CD can still deploy anything cluster-wide.

threats.title: Secrets readable cluster-wide
threats.description: Kubernetes Secrets are base64 only; broad RBAC (get secrets) or unencrypted etcd exposes them.
threats.mitigation: Least-privilege RBAC, etcd encryption at rest, mount only what each pod needs (separate migration secret from app secret).

threats.title: Weak pod and network hardening
threats.description: Without securityContext and NetworkPolicies, a compromise of the API can pivot to Kafka, Redis, ES and Postgres, which mostly lack their own auth.
threats.mitigation: Fixed: the app Deployment now sets runAsNonRoot/runAsUser/seccompProfile at pod level and allowPrivilegeEscalation=false/readOnlyRootFilesystem/capabilities-drop-ALL at container level, with an emptyDir at /tmp for the ONNX cache and JVM scratch writes. Each backing service (Postgres/Kafka/Redis/ES/Keycloak) now has a default-deny NetworkPolicy allowing ingress only from the app's pod label, closing the actual pivot path this threat describes. Residual: egress from the app pod is intentionally left unrestricted (plain Kubernetes NetworkPolicy can't express FQDN-based egress rules for OpenAI without a DNS-aware CNI like Cilium), so the 'explicit egress' half of the original mitigation isn't done. Verified: a disposable kind cluster + a single pod with the exact same securityContext confirmed the ONNX native library (.so) can still execute from the /tmp emptyDir -- a real Docker --tmpfs test initially showed a false failure (Docker's --tmpfs defaults to noexec, which kind's emptyDir does not).
